L763@P14: The jump mean and volatilities are calculated only over days where a jump is detected. Wright and Zhou (2009)
L764@P14-15: take one-month rolling window for realized volatility, since it can be estimated accurately with a fixed span of 16
L765@P15: sufficiently high-frequency data. Also for realized volatility you have one observation for every day. This is
L766@P15: certainly not the case for jumps; given the presumption that jumps in asset prices are both rare and large. Wright
L767@P15: and Zhou (2009) therefore argue that you need much longer rolling window for calculating the jump mean,
L768@P15: jump volatility and jump intensity. They take the parameter h equal to 24 months or 12 months. The tradeoff in
L769@P15-16: choosing h is that a shorter window gives a noisier but also timelier measure of agents’ perceptions of jump risk. 17
L770@P16: 5. Replication Wright and Zhou
L771@P16: In this section we replicate the results of Wright and Zhou (2009). The first objective is to see whether we get
L772@P16: similar results. Notice that we can not exactly replicate their findings, since we have a different sample period
L773@P16: and our analysis is based on the 10-year US future while Wright and Zhou (2009) use the 30 year future.

L2148@P39: years of the out-of-sample period there is no excess return, but this strategy shows very high returns in 2007 and

L2267@P41: 11. Recommendation for further research
L2268@P41: The analysis in this paper is based on the US market. An extension could be to look at other countries as well (for
L2269@P41: example UK, Germany and Japan) and see whether the results are robust over different countries.
L2270@P41: In this paper we presented already some robustness checks. There are more checks possible. For example, the yvariable presented here was the average excess return of the 2, 3, 4 and 5 year US bond. You could also take the
L2271@P41: return of the 10-year future as the y-variable. For the regression models, we looked at one-year holding period at
L2272@P41: monthly frequency. This means that there are 12 overlapping periods, which can cause statistical problems11. To
L2273@P41: avoid this, you can run a regression using only non-overlapping data.
L2274@P41: In the event plots presented in chapter 9 we did not take into account overnight returns, which could be
L2275@P41: important for the overall results. You can expand our analysis here by also considering this feature. However,
L2276@P41: with future data you have always to be careful with overnight returns because of rolling effects12. Therefore, in
L2277@P41: case of big overnight returns you have to investigate whether this was caused by changing market circumstances
L2278@P41: or because of the effects of rolling into a new contract.
L2279@P41: Again for the event plots we looked at all the 7:30 and 9:00 jumps. A next step could be to differentiate between
L2280@P41: jump event plots by considering which macro-economic news announcement caused a jump. For example have

L371@P7: potential source of risk. Our paper therefore adds to recent discussions on limited dealer
L372@P7: capacity and the resilience of the UST market (Duffie 2023; Duffie et al. 2023), and, more
L373@P7: broadly, to studies on UST liquidity (Hu, Pan, and Wang 2013) and UST term premium
L374@P7: (Adrian et al. 2013; Kim and Wright 2005).
L375@P7: We also contribute to the literature on U.S. Treasury by showing that demand for UST
L376@P7: safety helps explain time-series variations in Treasury convenience yields, including the Treasury basis (Du, Im, and Schreger 2018; Jiang, Krishnamurthy, and Lustig 2023; Acharya and
L377@P7: Laarits 2023) and Treasury-swap spreads (Adrian, Fleming, Shachar, and Vogt 2017). Our
L378@P7: observation that UST can abruptly swing from a safe-haven asset to a source of risk is consistent with the notation of Treasury inconvenience yields, as documented by He, Nagel, and
L379@P7: Song (2022) during the Covid-19 period. Additionally, our paper provides new insights into
L380@P7: the relationship between the safety of UST and USD, showing that it is UST safety, rather
L381@P7: than USD safety, that drives the UST convenience.
L382@P7: Our paper complements the literature on flights-to-safety,5 and is closely related to the
L383@P7: recent paper by Baele, Bekaert, Inghelbrecht, and Wei (2019), which uses multiple criteria
L384@P7: 4Specifically, we proxy intraday UST returns using 5-minute returns on 10-year Treasury futures, and
L385@P7: intraday SPX returns using 5-minute returns on E-mini S&P 500 futures.
L386@P7: 5See, for example, Connolly, Stivers, and Sun (2005), Baur and Lucey (2009), Baele, Bekaert, and
L387@P7: Inghelbrecht (2010), Bansal, Connolly, and Stivers (2010), Goyenko and Sarkissian (2014), Beber, Brandt,
L388@P7: and Cen (2014), Adrian, Crump, and Vogt (2019), among others.
L389@P7-8: 7such as return impact, correlation, and volatility spikes in global equity and bond markets
L390@P8: to identify flight-to-safety episodes. We take a different approach by constructing a simple
L391@P8: stock-bond correlation measure that, unlike Baele, Bekaert, Inghelbrecht, and Wei (2019),
L392@P8: captures not only flight-to-safety episodes but also bond risky episodes when UST becomes a
L393@P8: source of risk. Our finding on the UST and USD co-movement aligns with Kekre and Lenel
L394@P8: (2024), who show theoretically that flight-to-safety episodes lead to dollar appreciation and
L395@P8: global output declines under nominal rigidity.
L396@P8: Finally, our paper adds to the literature on the stock-bond correlation. Existing papers,
L397@P8: including Campbell, Pflueger, and Viceira (2020), David and Veronesi (2013), D.E.Shaw
L398@P8: (2019), Cieslak and Schrimpf (2019), Ermolov (2022), Laarits (2022), and Li, Zha, Zhang,
L399@P8: and Zhou (2022), have proposed different channels to explain the time-variations in the stockbond correlations. We build on these observation to construct our measure and explore the
L400@P8: information contained in the daily variations of the stock-bond correlations.
L401@P8: The rest of our paper is organized as follows. Section 2 describes the construction of the
L402@P8: safety measure and the characteristics of the flight-to-UST episodes. Section 3 and Section 4
L403@P8: investigate asset pricing under Bond Safety and Risky Days. Section 5 concludes the paper.
L404@P8: Further details are provided in the appendices.
